name: The WEF AI-First Operating System
blurb:
The World Economic Forum published The AI-First Operating System in June 2026, produced with Kearney under its AI-First Enterprises workstream and drawing on more than 50 enterprises and thinkers.

Its central claim is worth stating precisely, because it differs from most enterprise AI guidance. The paper argues that general purpose technologies, electricity, computers, the internet, had limited effect when incumbents applied them inside existing systems, and that the breakthroughs came when firms rebuilt around the technology. It applies the same reading to AI: adopting AI as a tool is a different activity from designing an operating logic around it, and only the second produces the compounding effects the paper describes.

The five building blocks are the intelligence engine, the adaptive AI technology stack, operations redesign, human-AI teaming, and new value creation. The paper extends the traditional business model canvas with AI-first fundamentals so leaders can work through them against their own organisation.

Two things about its framing are unusual and worth noting. The authors state plainly that these blocks are not a transformation roadmap, they are a description of how the frontier already operates. And they concede openly that it remains unclear which approaches will prove effective across industries, how broadly they will scale, or what the long-term implications are for productivity, employment and competition. That is more candid than most frameworks in this category.

points.desc: The paper places AI alongside electricity, computers and the internet as a general purpose technology, and argues each had limited impact while incumbents applied it inside existing systems. The breakthroughs came from firms that rebuilt around the technology. That is the distinction between an AI tool programme and an AI-first operating model.
points.name: The thesis: rebuilding beats adopting

points.desc: Intelligence at the centre of operations and business model, so every interaction compounds. The paper breaks it into three loops: speed, scale and scope.
points.name: Block 1: the intelligence engine

points.desc: Modular architecture integrating data, models and workflows, designed to change as the frontier moves. The paper is specific about owning the control layers and keeping a model-agnostic portfolio rather than committing to one provider.
points.name: Block 2: an adaptive technology stack

points.desc: Connecting all operations to the intelligence engine rather than improving workflows at the margins. The paper treats where to allocate intelligence as a deliberate allocation decision, the same way capital is allocated.
points.name: Block 3: operations redesign, not optimisation

points.desc: Roles, teams and structures designed for continuous collaboration between people and AI systems, and an explicit attempt to define what the human contribution is at the frontier rather than leaving it as a residual.
points.name: Block 4: human-AI teaming

points.desc: Every AI-first organisation has to decide how it positions intelligence in the market, from AI as a visible product feature to AI as invisible infrastructure. The paper argues that choice determines where value accrues and how the business competes, which makes it a strategy decision rather than a marketing one.
points.name: Block 5: positioning determines what customers pay for

points.desc: The paper states that the rise of AI-first enterprises is early, that it is unclear which approaches will prove most effective across industries, how broadly they will scale, or what the long-term implications are for productivity, employment and competition. A framework that names its own uncertainty is rarer than it should be, and worth weighing against ones that do not.
points.name: It says what it does not know

reading.body:
The World Economic Forum's June 2026 AI-First Operating System argues that rebuilding a company around AI produces compounding effects that adopting AI as a tool does not.

The paper's central move is an analogy to earlier general purpose technologies. Electricity, computers and the internet had limited effect, it argues, while incumbents applied them inside existing systems, and the breakthroughs came from firms that rebuilt around them. Applied to AI, that yields a distinction between an AI tool programme and an AI-first operating model. The five building blocks follow from it: an intelligence engine at the centre of operations, an adaptive technology stack, operations redesigned rather than optimised at the margins, human-AI teaming, and a decision about how intelligence is positioned in the market. Two of the blocks carry specific operational advice. The stack should keep a model-agnostic portfolio and own the control layers rather than committing to one provider. Operations should treat where to allocate intelligence as a deliberate allocation decision, the same way capital is allocated. The paper was produced with Kearney and draws on more than 50 enterprises and thinkers.

For AI specifically, the framework's claim is that the returns depend on where intelligence sits in the business rather than on which models are used. Block five makes this explicit: whether AI appears as a visible product feature or as invisible infrastructure determines where value accrues and how the business competes, which the paper treats as strategy rather than marketing. That reframes the common enterprise question from which model to buy to what the operating logic is built around.

What the data does not contain is any measurement. There are no cost figures, no productivity results, no industry breakdown, and no evidence that the five blocks produce the compounding the paper describes. The paper itself concedes that the rise of AI-first enterprises is early and that it is unclear which approaches will prove effective across industries, how broadly they will scale, or what the long-term implications are for productivity, employment and competition. It also says nothing about compute, power or physical infrastructure, so it cannot speak to whether the operating model it describes is constrained by what those layers can supply. It is a description of how the frontier operates, by its own account, not a roadmap and not a result.

The mechanism behind the five blocks is that they are not independent fixes. The intelligence engine sits at the centre of operations and business model, and operations redesign connects all operations to it, so the compounding the paper describes comes from every interaction feeding the speed, scale and scope loops rather than from any single tool. The adaptive stack's instruction to own the control layers and keep a model-agnostic portfolio is the practical consequence: if the frontier moves, an enterprise committed to one provider cannot reallocate intelligence where the operating logic needs it.

The comparison the data supports is between positioning intelligence as a visible product feature and as invisible infrastructure. That choice determines where value accrues and how the business competes, so two firms with the same models can end up with different economics depending on where intelligence sits. The paper's own concession that it is unclear which approaches will scale across industries is the mechanism that limits the framework: it describes how the frontier operates, not which parts of that description will hold.

What are the five building blocks in the WEF AI-First Operating System?
The intelligence engine, the adaptive AI technology stack, operations redesign, human-AI teaming, and new value creation. The paper extends the traditional business model canvas with AI-first fundamentals so leaders can work through them against their own organisation.

Who produced the paper and when?
The World Economic Forum published it in June 2026, produced with Kearney under its AI-First Enterprises workstream. It draws on more than 50 enterprises and thinkers.

Does the paper recommend committing to one AI model provider?
No. The paper is specific about owning the control layers and keeping a model-agnostic portfolio rather than committing to one provider.

Does the paper provide evidence that rebuilding around AI produces compounding effects?
No. The data contains no cost figures, productivity results, industry breakdown, or evidence that the five blocks produce the compounding the paper describes. The paper itself concedes that the rise of AI-first enterprises is early and it is unclear which approaches will prove effective across industries.

What does the paper say about compute, power, or physical infrastructure constraints?
The data contains nothing about compute, power or physical infrastructure. The paper cannot speak to whether the operating model it describes is constrained by what those layers can supply.

What are the three loops of the intelligence engine?
Speed, scale and scope. The intelligence engine places intelligence at the centre of operations and business model so every interaction compounds.

summary: A June 2026 World Economic Forum white paper, with Kearney, describing how enterprises that redesigned around AI actually operate. Five building blocks, drawn from more than 50 companies, and an explicit statement that it is a description of the frontier rather than a roadmap.
